plan.contextChunk: This figure contains six panels (a)–(f) illustrating the operation of insertion sort on an array of six integers. Each panel shows a horizontal array of six cells indexed 1 through 6 above the cells. Gray cells to the left of the current key represent the already-sorted subarray; the current key is shown in a black cell with white text; white cells to the right remain unsorted. Curved arrows below the array indicate element movements: a bold black arrow points to the slot where the key will be inserted, while lighter gray arrows indicate elements shifting one position to the right to make room. Panel (a) shows the initial array [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] with key 2 at position 2 moving left past 5. Panel (b) shows key 4 at position 3 being inserted into sorted subarray [2, 5]. Panel (c) shows key 6 at position 4 requiring no movement as it is already the largest element in the sorted prefix. Panel (d) shows key 1 at position 5 shifting four elements rightward to reach position 1. Panel (e) shows key 3 at position 6 shifting three elements rightward to reach its correct position. Panel (f) shows the final sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] with no black cell and no arrows. This figure illustrates the insertion sort algorithm step by step, demonstrating how each key is extracted and inserted into its correct position within the growing sorted subarray to its left.

interactionPlan.concept: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by taking the next key and moving it left past larger elements until it reaches its correct position.

interactions.teaches: the learner understands the exact order in which insertion sort compares adjacent values, moves the key left, and expands the sorted prefix.
interactions.label: Edit insertionSort()

api.does: return the number of array cells
return true when A[i] > A[j], and highlight the two compared cells
move the current key at index i one position left while the displaced element moves one position right; this is the only way to mutate the array
highlight index i as the current key in black; markKey(0) clears the key highlight
shade cells 1 through k gray to show the sorted prefix
attach a short learner-written annotation to the current replay frame

interactions.frame: the whole six-cell array with index labels, the gray sorted prefix, the black current key, compared indices, and any arrow caused by the latest shift
interactions.success_check: the final array is in nondecreasing order and the replay shows the sorted prefix expanding from one cell to all six cells

demo_steps.title: Start with one sorted cell
demo_steps.narration: The first element alone is already sorted, so the gray prefix begins with just index 1. The next element becomes the black key.

demo_steps.title: Move a small key left
demo_steps.narration: When the key 2 is compared with 5, the comparison is true because 5 > 2. A shift moves the key left and pushes 5 right, producing the sorted prefix [2, 5].

demo_steps.title: Stop when order is correct
demo_steps.narration: For key 4, the algorithm shifts past 5 but stops before 2 because 2 is not greater than 4. The key is inserted exactly where the sorted order changes.

demo_steps.title: Notice the no-shift case
demo_steps.narration: Key 6 is already larger than everything in the sorted prefix, so the while loop performs no shifts. Insertion sort can sometimes expand the prefix with only one failed comparison.

demo_steps.title: Watch many shifts make one insertion
demo_steps.narration: Key 1 must move left past 6, 5, 4, and 2, so several adjacent shifts represent one insertion into the front of the prefix.

demo_steps.title: Finish the sorted array
demo_steps.narration: The final key 3 moves left until it belongs between 2 and 4. When every prefix cell is gray and no black key remains, the array is sorted.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Insertion sort never sorts the whole array at once; it maintains a sorted prefix and inserts one new key into that prefix on each pass.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean black-and-white textbook style with large serif numerals. Each array is a row of six outlined boxes with indices above. Gray fill means the already-sorted prefix, black fill with white text means the current key, and white cells are not yet processed. Curved arrows below the cells should show the key’s insertion path in black and the displaced elements’ rightward shifts in gray. The interactive replay should preserve this visual language while showing one execution frame at a time beside the learner’s code editor.
